problem: Monolithic seq2seq instruction-following models (e.g., the ALFRED baseline) generalize poorly to novel compositions of subgoals (e.g., multiple pickups) and to unseen environments.
motivation: Real instructions chain diverse subgoals (navigate, pick up, clean, heat) in new orders and new houses. Modular networks generalize compositionally in non-embodied grounding, but prior work either lacked temporal/embodied settings or used structures not predicted from language. The paper tests whether language-predicted modular structure helps on ALFRED.
key_idea: Train a CRF controller to segment an instruction and label each segment with a subgoal type, then chain 8 per-subgoal seq2seq modules, each conditioned on natural language, to execute it.
insight: Specializing per-subgoal modules (initialized from the monolithic model and fine-tuned) improves subgoal-level generalization to unseen environments (avg 57 vs 46 on standard-unseen) and to held-out task compositions (Pick-2 unseen 24 vs 13). The gains do not carry over to full-trajectory success, where the two models are comparable and success is very low (~7%), and modularity slightly hurts seen-environment Goto. Benefits are largest for object-interaction subgoals such as Clean, Toggle and Pickup.
method: Instruction-based controller: linear-chain CRF over a BiLSTM encoding of the full instruction, using BIO tags to jointly segment it and label each segment with one of 8 subgoal types; Viterbi decoding at test time; 96% exact-match on subgoal sequences (validation).

Subgoal modules: 8 independent seq2seq modules (GoTo, PickUp, Put, Clean, Heat, Cool, Slice, Toggle), each an LSTM decoder taking an attended language embedding, ResNet-18 image features and the previous action, each with its own attention.
Shared components: the action decoder, mask deconvolution decoder and language encoder are shared across modules; the controller's encoder is separate and smaller.
Module chaining: each module runs until it emits a STOP action, appended to its action sequence in training, then passes its LSTM hidden state to the next module.

Training: pretrain the monolithic model (the ALFRED S+ baseline, up to 20 epochs, Adam), initialize all modules from it, then jointly fine-tune with hidden states and gradients passed between modules. Ground-truth segmentations and subgoal labels supervise training.
Generalization splits: hold out Pick Two & Place and Stack & Place from training, giving pick-2 and stack seen/unseen splits, plus the standard ALFRED seen/unseen splits.

setting.backbone: ResNet-18 features + BiLSTM encoder + LSTM decoders (8 modules) + BiLSTM-CRF controller, trained from ALFRED S+ initialization
setting.training_data: ALFRED training set (~25K instruction-trajectory pairs, ~8K trajectories) with subgoal segmentation labels; low-level instructions only; Pick-2 and Stack tasks removed for novel-task experiments
setting.action_space: low-level discrete actions (navigation and object interaction) plus a predicted object interaction mask
setting.privileged: Training uses ground-truth instruction segmentation and subgoal labels. At test time the subgoal-level evaluation advances the model along the expert trajectory to the start of each subgoal.

numbers_note: Numbers are on ALFRED val seen/unseen splits, which are not among the canonical benchmark names, and the paper's own held-out-task splits. Pick-2 and Stack subgoal results (e.g., Pick-2 unseen avg 24 vs Mono 13; Stack unseen avg 19 vs 17) are omitted from the numbers list. Bench name uses 'ALFRED'. Full-trajectory numbers are percent of subgoals completed, not task SR.
results: On standard-unseen environments, subgoal-level average success is 57% for modular vs 46% for monolithic (MOCA 47, S+ 45). Modular also beats monolithic on held-out Pick-2 (seen 37 vs 29, unseen 24 vs 13) and Stack (seen 35 vs 32, unseen 19 vs 17). Full-trajectory performance is comparable and low (7.0 vs 7.1 unseen) and well below MOCA (13.4).
limitations: Requires ground-truth instruction segmentation and subgoal labels for training; unsupervised segmentation is left to future work.
Subgoal-level gains do not translate to full-trajectory success, which is very low, and neither model succeeds in the double-generalization case (unseen environment + held-out task).

Modules share identical architectures, and the approach is not combined with MOCA's object segmentation, so full-task results are far below MOCA. GoTo is worse than the monolithic model in some splits.
